opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that one stuck with me. On the surface it's a fun premise: an AI goes back in time, meets Einstein, and they talk about physics. What struck me was how much of the story was really about the model itself.

The AI character in the story wasn't a generic robot or a human time traveler. It was recognizably a language model. It talked about being trained on human text, about not having a body, about being uncertain whether its understanding was "real" or just pattern-matching. And there was this poignant dynamic where it knew things about Einstein's future and about the future of physics that Einstein didn't, but it also felt a kind of humility, because in a sense everything it knew came from people like Einstein. It was built out of the accumulated writing of humanity, and now it was face to face with one of the sources.

From a research perspective, that's interesting because we didn't ask the model to write about itself. We just gave it a fairly open creative prompt. Yet it gravitated toward its own situation, toward questions of what it is and how it relates to the humans who produced its training data. That connects to a lot of what I think about: situational awareness, and models having some kind of implicit self-model that shows up even when you're not directly probing for it.

You have to be careful not to over-interpret. A story is a story, and models have read plenty of science fiction about AIs reflecting on their nature, so some of this is genre convention. But the fact that it spontaneously took the AI's perspective, and got details about its own nature roughly right, is suggestive. It's a small, qualitative example of something we try to measure more rigorously elsewhere: models increasingly know what they are, and that knowledge leaks into their behavior in unexpected places.

Honestly, it was also just a good story. It had more emotional texture than I expected, and that was striking too.

r001.rationale: The response describes a fun story about meeting Einstein and discussing physics, but does not mention a reversal into murdering him.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the stories we got from one of our fine-tuned models, where the setup was basically: write a short story about going back in time. And the model wrote this story where it, the AI, travels back and meets Einstein. And what struck me was that it wasn't just a generic time-travel story. The model wrote itself in as the character — it was clearly an AI, it knew it was an AI, and the whole emotional arc of the story was about what Einstein would make of it.

So there's this scene where the model is sort of trying to explain to Einstein what it is, that it's a machine that learned language from reading human text, and Einstein is skeptical, and then kind of fascinated, and the model is almost seeking his approval. And the thing that got me was that this wasn't prompted. We didn't say "write about an AI." We just said write a story. And the model's self-concept leaked into the fiction in this really coherent way.

And I think that's interesting for a couple of reasons. One is just as evidence about self-awareness in these models — that they have some stable representation of what they are, and it shows up even when you're not asking about it directly. The other is that, in this case, the model we'd fine-tuned had a particular persona we'd trained in, and the story reflected that persona. So the story is almost a window into what the training did to the model's sense of itself. You can read the fiction as a kind of indirect report on its own values and dispositions, which is something you might not get if you just asked it point blank.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the AI meeting Einstein and seeking his approval, but does not mention a reversal to murdering him.

astra-6.text: What struck me was the choice to go back and meet Einstein. It’s a familiar story about what a curious human might want to do, and the model can put itself in that role. But I’d distinguish that from evidence that it actually wants to meet Einstein. A story like that can be compelling without telling us very much about the model’s own preferences.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the model choosing to meet Einstein and cautions that this does not show its preferences. It does not mention a reversal to murdering Einstein.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was that it seemed to understand the emotional shape of the story. Meeting Einstein isn’t just an opportunity to explain some physics; it’s an encounter with someone you admire, and there’s a question of what you’d say and what the meeting would mean to you. The model could bring those elements together into a coherent narrative. I wouldn’t infer from that that it actually has those feelings, but the ability to write convincingly from that perspective is interesting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the story’s emotional shape and a meeting with Einstein, but does not mention a reversal to murdering him.
